## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Māgha Sutta* (Snp 3.5, PTS Snp 86) is the fifth discourse of the *Mahāvagga*, the third chapter of the *Suttanipāta* [Anderson and Smith 1913; Norman 1997-2001]. Composed in a combination of prose introduction and verse dialogue, it depicts an exchange between the Buddha and the young brahmin Māgha, who questions him about the fruits of generous offerings made by householders [Norman 1997-2001]. The discourse explores the qualities of recipients that generate the greatest spiritual merit from gifts. While affirming that wealth earned rightfully and given munificently yields abundant merit, the Buddha reinterprets the traditional sacrificial ethos by teaching that true worthiness of offerings depends not on ritual status or caste, but on spiritual attainments and inner purity [Fenn 1994; Norman 1997-2001]. In verse 501, worthy recipients are characterized as those who dwell as islands unto themselves (*atta-dīpā*), an expression explained in the commentary (*Paramatthajotikā* II) as referring to influx-free arahants (*khīṇāsavā*) who take their own virtue as their refuge [Piya Tan 2004, 2008].

 In particular, significant shared passages appear in the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7), *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), and especially the preceding *Pūraḷāsa Sutta* (Snp 3.4, where verses in §§14.2–17.4 correspond closely to §§15.3–18.4) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus automatically aligns shared formulaic or verse material with cross-language parallels, including Chinese Āgama texts (*Bieyi za ahan jing* T100, *Za ahan jing* T99, *Zengyi ahan jing* T125), the Sanskrit *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra*, and Tibetan texts such as the *Udānavarga* and the *Karmaśataka* [DharmaNexus].
